claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2016, Le et al., 2016, and Sharkey et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Brain-directed expression of wild-type UBQLN2 toxicity is potentially due to disruptions in Ub homeostasis.
claims.source: Brain-directed expression of wild-type UBQLN2 also caused toxicity phenotypes (Huang et al., 2016; Le et al., 2016; Sharkey et al., 2020), potentially due to disruptions in Ub homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed toxicity.

claims.claim: UBQLN2 harbors low complexity regions and undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation.
claims.source: Finally, like many proteins implicated in ALS/FTD (Pakravan et al., 2021), UBQLN2 harbors low complexity regions and undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (Sharkey et al., 2018; Dao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Sharkey et al., 2018 and Dao et al., 2018.

claims.claim: ALS-associated mutations in the PRR may interfere with UBQLN2 liquid demixing.
claims.source: While ALS-associated mutations in the PRR may interfere with UBQLN2 liquid demixing, the relevance to disease pathogenesis is presently unclear.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential mechanism.

claims.claim: The relevance of UBQLN2 liquid demixing interference to disease pathogenesis is presently unclear.
claims.source: While ALS-associated mutations in the PRR may interfere with UBQLN2 liquid demixing, the relevance to disease pathogenesis is presently unclear.
claims.evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Expression of ALS-associated UBQLN2 mutants caused mutation-dependent neurotoxicity in Drosophila.
claims.source: In previous work, we reported that expression of ALS-associated UBQLN2 mutants caused mutation-dependent neurotoxicity in Drosophila (Kim et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claims.claim: Endolysosomal dysfunction and axon guidance defects are phenotypic drivers of neurodegeneration in UBQLN2-associated ALS/FTD.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that endolysosomal dysfunction and axon guidance defects are phenotypic drivers of neurodegeneration in UBQLN2-associated ALS/FTD.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the combined findings.

claims.claim: Homozygous expression of single-copy human UBQLN2ALS alleles caused mild eye toxicity when expressed under control of an eye-specific GMR driver at 22°C.
claims.source: We previously reported that homozygous expression of single-copy human UBQLN2ALS alleles caused mild eye toxicity when expressed under control of an eye-specific GMR driver at 22°C (Kim et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claims.claim: UBQLN2-associated phenotypes may be worsened by heat stress.
claims.source: Reasoning that UBQLN2-associated phenotypes may be worsened by heat stress (HS), we compared eye morphologies between flies expressing UBQLN2WT, a clinical UBQLN2P497H allele, and a highly aggregation-prone UBQLN24XALS mutant that harbors four different clinical mutations (P497H, P506T, P509S, and P525S, Figure 1A; Kim et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is the reasoning behind the experimental design.

claims.claim: None of the UBQLN2 transgenes caused an overt external eye phenotype when expressed from a hemizygous GMR>UBQLN2 Chr2 locus at 22°C.
claims.source: None of the UBQLN2 transgenes caused an overt external eye phenotype when expressed from a hemizygous GMR>UBQLN2 Chr2 locus at 22°C (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited a moderately severe rough eye (RE) phenotype characterized by eye depigmentation and loss of ommatidial facets in both male and female flies at 29°C.
claims.source: By contrast, GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies—but not GMR>UBQLN2WT or GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies—exhibited a moderately severe rough eye (RE) phenotype that was characterized by eye depigmentation and loss of ommatidial facets in both male and female flies (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: UBQLN24XALS was significantly less soluble than UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H at both 22°C and 29°C.
claims.source: As expected, UBQLN24XALS was significantly less soluble than UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H at both 22°C and 29°C; however, the relative proportion of insoluble UBQLN24XALS was comparable at both temperatures, suggesting that increased aggregation of UBQLN24XALS cannot wholly account for its enhanced toxicity at 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: The relative proportion of insoluble UBQLN24XALS was comparable at both 22°C and 29°C.
claims.source: As expected, UBQLN24XALS was significantly less soluble than UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H at both 22°C and 29°C; however, the relative proportion of insoluble UBQLN24XALS was comparable at both temperatures, suggesting that increased aggregation of UBQLN24XALS cannot wholly account for its enhanced toxicity at 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: Increased aggregation of UBQLN24XALS cannot wholly account for its enhanced toxicity at 29°C.
claims.source: As expected, UBQLN24XALS was significantly less soluble than UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H at both 22°C and 29°C; however, the relative proportion of insoluble UBQLN24XALS was comparable at both temperatures, suggesting that increased aggregation of UBQLN24XALS cannot wholly account for its enhanced toxicity at 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the solubility data.

claims.claim: The average number of peptide spectral matches for hUBQLN2 was comparable between GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 22°C and 29°C.
claims.source: The average number of peptide spectral matches for hUBQLN2 was comparable between GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 22°C and 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: hUBQLN2-unique peptides were ~6-fold more abundant than dUbqln peptides in both GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS heads.
claims.source: hUBQLN2-unique peptides were ~6-fold more abundant than dUbqln peptides in both GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS heads, providing a lower limit of hUBQLN2 overexpression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Absolute numbers of hUBQLN2 peptides were higher in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C versus 22°C.
claims.source: As expected, given the heat inducibility of UAS, absolute numbers of hUBQLN2 peptides were higher in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C versus 22°C; however, the difference was not statistically significant across three replicates.
claims.evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: The difference in hUBQLN2 peptide abundance between 29°C and 22°C was not statistically significant across three replicates.
claims.source: As expected, given the heat inducibility of UAS, absolute numbers of hUBQLN2 peptides were higher in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C versus 22°C; however, the difference was not statistically significant across three replicates.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: Each of the three GMR>UBQLN2 lines exhibited hundreds of gene expression changes relative to GMR-Gal4 controls.
claims.source: Each of the three GMR>UBQLN2 lines exhibited hundreds of gene expression changes relative to GMR-Gal4 controls, suggesting that UBQLN2 overexpression has a substantial impact on cellular regulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: UBQLN2 overexpression has a substantial impact on cellular regulation.
claims.source: Each of the three GMR>UBQLN2 lines exhibited hundreds of gene expression changes relative to GMR-Gal4 controls, suggesting that UBQLN2 overexpression has a substantial impact on cellular regulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited a distinct RNA-Seq gene expression signature relative to GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies.
claims.source: Consistent with their more severe eye phenotype, GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited a distinct RNA-Seq gene expression signature relative to GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies, which clustered together in principle component analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: 629 genes were uniquely changed in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies versus GMR>UBQLN2WT, GMR>UBQLN2P497H, and GMR-Gal4 controls at 29°C.
claims.source: Using an FDR of <0.05, 629 genes were uniquely changed in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies versus GMR>UBQLN2WT, GMR>UBQLN2P497H, and GMR-Gal4 controls at 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: 402 genes were upregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies.
claims.source: Of these, 402 genes were upregulated and 227 genes were downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 1 and 2, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E.

claims.claim: 227 genes were downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies.
claims.source: Of these, 402 genes were upregulated and 227 genes were downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 1 and 2, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E.

claims.claim: mRNAs involved in eye development and phototransduction, including inaC, ninaE, and Rh3, were broadly downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies, likely reflecting degenerative cell loss.
claims.source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis revealed that mRNAs involved in eye development and phototransduction, including inaC, ninaE, and Rh3, were broadly downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies, likely reflecting degenerative cell loss (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on GO analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Upregulated GO terms in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies included response to biotic stimulus, which includes Drosophila innate immunity genes such as Dro, AttB, AttC, and Listericin.
claims.source: Upregulated GO terms included response to biotic stimulus, which includes Drosophila innate immunity genes such as Dro, AttB, AttC, and Listericin, and response to UV light, which includes the small heat-shock protein-encoding genes Hsp23, Hsp26, and Hsp27 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on GO analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Upregulated GO terms in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies included response to UV light, which includes the small heat-shock protein-encoding genes Hsp23, Hsp26, and Hsp27.
claims.source: Upregulated GO terms included response to biotic stimulus, which includes Drosophila innate immunity genes such as Dro, AttB, AttC, and Listericin, and response to UV light, which includes the small heat-shock protein-encoding genes Hsp23, Hsp26, and Hsp27 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on GO analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Upregulation of HSPs may be driven by UBQLN24XALS misfolding.
claims.source: Upregulation of HSPs may be driven by UBQLN24XALS misfolding.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed upregulation of HSPs.

claims.claim: Only 64 genes were differentially expressed between GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies.
claims.source: In contrast to the profound differences between GMR>UBQLN24XALS and GMR>UBQLN2WT flies, only 64 genes were differentially expressed between GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies, which is consistent with their qualitatively similar eye phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: 28 differentially expressed genes were common to GMR>UBQLN24XALS and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies relative to GMR>UBQLN2WT flies.
claims.source: Finally, 28 differentially expressed genes were common to GMR>UBQLN24XALS and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies relative to GMR>UBQLN2WT flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claims.claim: The strong eye phenotype of GMR>UBQLN24XALS is accompanied by robust changes in gene expression.
claims.source: Overall, these findings reveal that the strong eye phenotype of GMR>UBQLN24XALS is accompanied by robust changes in gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on the RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: A Bloomington Df library of 194 lines spanning 85% of chromosome 2 was screened for UBQLN2ALS modifiers.
claims.source: To this end, we screened a Bloomington Df library of 194 lines spanning 85% of chromosome 2 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This describes the genetic screen methodology.

claims.claim: The UBQLN24XALS screen identified seven suppressors.
claims.source: The UBQLN24XALS screen identified seven suppressors, three of which overlapped a common genomic interval, and 23 enhancers, including 15 lethal enhancers (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The UBQLN24XALS screen identified 23 enhancers, including 15 lethal enhancers.
claims.source: The UBQLN24XALS screen identified seven suppressors, three of which overlapped a common genomic interval, and 23 enhancers, including 15 lethal enhancers (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The UBQLN2P497H screen identified six enhancers, two of which were also identified in the UBQLN24XALS screen.
claims.source: The UBQLN2P497H screen identified six enhancers, two of which were also identified in the UBQLN24XALS screen (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: All Dfs that enhanced the GMR>UBQLN2P497H eye phenotype also caused enhanced eye phenotypes in GMR>UBQLN2WT flies.
claims.source: Notably, all Dfs that enhanced the GMR>UBQLN2P497H eye phenotype also caused enhanced eye phenotypes in GMR>UBQLN2WT flies.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the genetic screen.

claims.claim: Rab5 knockdown phenocopied the hyperpigmented phenotype seen in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to BSC37 at 29°C.
claims.source: In support of a role for Rab5 as a UBQLN2 modifier gene, Rab5 knockdown phenocopied the hyperpigmented phenotype seen in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to BSC37 at 29°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claims.claim: Rab5 knockdown caused a hyperpigmented eye phenotype in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies.
claims.source: Rab5 knockdown also caused a hyperpigmented eye phenotype in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating Rab5 is a mutation-independent UBQLN2 enhancer.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Rab5 is a mutation-independent UBQLN2 enhancer.
claims.source: Rab5 knockdown also caused a hyperpigmented eye phenotype in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating Rab5 is a mutation-independent UBQLN2 enhancer.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Rab5 knockdown affects all UBQLN2 variants.

claims.claim: GMR>UBQLN24XALS/shRab5 flies reared at 22°C failed to exhibit eye patches.
claims.source: Interestingly, while Rab5 knockdown also caused hyperpigmented eye patches in GMR>UBQLN2WT, and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies reared at 22°C, GMR>UBQLN24XALS/shRab5 flies reared at 22°C failed to exhibit eye patches (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: UBQLN24XALS phenotypes are heat stress dependent.
claims.source: This finding supports the idea that UBQLN24XALS phenotypes are HS dependent and is consistent with an earlier study showing stronger eye phenotypes in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies relative to GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies at 22°C (Kim et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the temperature-dependent phenotypes and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Overexpression of GFP-Rab5 partially rescued the eye phenotype of GMR>UBQLN2WT, GMR>UBQLN2P497H, and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C.
claims.source: Finally, we showed that overexpression of GFP-Rab5 partially rescued the eye phenotype of GMR>UBQLN2WT, GMR>UBQLN2P497H, and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Rab5 knockdown or overexpression did not affect UBQLN2 expression.
claims.source: Rab5 knockdown or overexpression did not affect UBQLN2 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E, G, H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E, G, H.

claims.claim: Rab5 is a general modulator of UBQLN2 toxicity.
claims.source: The combined findings suggest that Rab5 is a general modulator of UBQLN2 toxicity and that UBQLN2 overexpression interferes with endolysosomal function in flies.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the Rab5 experiments.

claims.claim: UBQLN2 overexpression interferes with endolysosomal function in flies.
claims.source: The combined findings suggest that Rab5 is a general modulator of UBQLN2 toxicity and that UBQLN2 overexpression interferes with endolysosomal function in flies.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the Rab5 experiments.

claims.claim: lilli encodes a transcriptional elongation factor that is orthologous to mammalian AF4/FMR2 (fragile X mental retardation 2).
claims.source: Within this overlap we identified lilliputian (lilli) as a gene of interest. lilli encodes a transcriptional elongation factor that is orthologous to mammalian AF4/FMR2 (fragile X mental retardation 2) (Wittwer et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wittwer et al., 2001.

claims.claim: lilli mutations were shown to suppress toxicity of TDP-43 and C9ORF72-derived dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) in Drosophila.
claims.source: Interestingly, lilli mutations were recently shown to suppress toxicity of TDP-43 and C9ORF72-derived dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) in Drosophila (Chung et al., 2018; Yuva-Aydemir et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2018 and Yuva-Aydemir et al., 2019.

claims.claim: A lilliA17-2 LOF allele diminished UBQLN24XALS-mediated eye toxicity to a similar extent as lilli-spanning Dfs.
claims.source: In support of lilli as a UBQLN24XALS suppressor, a lilliA17-2 LOF allele diminished UBQLN24XALS-mediated eye toxicity to a similar extent as lilli-spanning Dfs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C.

claims.claim: lilli may be of interest as a general suppressor of toxicity arising from misexpression of neurodegeneration-associated genes in Drosophila.
claims.source: Thus, lilli may be of interest as a general suppressor of toxicity arising from misexpression of neurodegeneration-associated genes in Drosophila.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that lilli suppresses multiple ALS-related proteins.

claims.claim: Unc-5 encodes a transmembrane dependence receptor that mediates axonal repulsion and apoptosis suppression in response to secreted netrin ligands.
claims.source: The region of overlap between ED2426 and BSC346 contains Unc-5, which encodes a transmembrane dependence receptor that mediates axonal repulsion and apoptosis suppression in response to secreted netrin ligands (Boyer and Gupton, 2018; Labrador et al., 2005; Keleman and Dickson, 2001; Llambi et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2009; Ahn et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing Unc-5 function.

claims.claim: Two Unc-5 LOF alleles and three different RNAi lines diminished the RE phenotype of GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies without affecting UBQLN2 expression.
claims.source: In support of a genetic interaction between Unc-5 and UBQLN24XALS, two Unc-5 LOF alleles (Labrador et al., 2005), and three different RNAi lines diminished the RE phenotype of GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies without affecting UBQLN2 expression (Figure 3C, D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C, D and E.

claims.claim: Unc-5 knockdown had no effect on the RE phenotype caused by the expression of ALS-associated FUS alleles.
claims.source: By contrast, Unc-5 knockdown had no effect on the RE phenotype caused by the expression of ALS-associated FUS alleles that cause severe degenerative phenotypes in Drosophila (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Lanson et al., 2011; Kwiatkowski et al., 2009; Vance et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claims.claim: Genetic interaction with Unc-5 may be specific to UBQLN2 versus other ectopically expressed ALS-associated proteins in Drosophila.
claims.source: This suggests that genetic interaction with Unc-5 may be specific to UBQLN2 versus other ectopically expressed ALS-associated proteins in Drosophila.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of the Unc-5 effect.

claims.claim: fra encodes the fly ortholog of mammalian deleted in colon carcinoma (DCC).
claims.source: The repulsive activity of Unc-5 on axon guidance is antagonized by frazzled (fra), which encodes the fly ortholog of mammalian deleted in colon carcinoma (DCC) (Chan et al., 1996; Keino-Masu et al., 1996; Kolodziej et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chan et al., 1996, Keino-Masu et al., 1996, and Kolodziej et al., 1996.

claims.claim: fra silencing rescued the UBQLN24XALS eye phenotype to a similar extent as Unc-5 knockdown.
claims.source: fra silencing by two different RNAi lines rescued the UBQLN24XALS eye phenotype to a similar extent as Unc-5 knockdown (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Signaling through Unc-5/Frazzled potentiates UBQLN24XALS toxicity in the Drosophila compound eye.
claims.source: The combined findings suggest that signaling through Unc-5/Frazzled potentiates UBQLN24XALS toxicity in the Drosophila compound eye.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data.

claims.claim: The moderate climbing defect of D42>UBQLN24XALS flies relative to D42-Gal4 flies was partially reversed by an shUnc-5 (TRiP) allele in both male and female flies.
claims.source: The moderate climbing defect of D42>UBQLN24XALS flies relative to D42-Gal4 flies was partially reversed by an shUnc-5 (TRiP) allele in both male and female flies, while a second Unc-5 shRNA line (KK) rescued climbing in male but not female flies (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: A second Unc-5 shRNA line (KK) rescued climbing in male but not female D42>UBQLN24XALS flies.
claims.source: The moderate climbing defect of D42>UBQLN24XALS flies relative to D42-Gal4 flies was partially reversed by an shUnc-5 (TRiP) allele in both male and female flies, while a second Unc-5 shRNA line (KK) rescued climbing in male but not female flies (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: D42>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited neuromuscular junction (NMJ) abnormalities, including increased numbers of satellite boutons and reduced numbers of mature boutons.
claims.source: Consistent with their climbing defects, D42>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited neuromuscular junction (NMJ) abnormalities, including increased numbers of satellite boutons and reduced numbers of mature boutons.
claims.evidence: This is based on NMJ morphology analysis.

claims.claim: NMJ abnormalities in D42>UBQLN24XALS flies were corrected by Unc-5 silencing.
claims.source: Both phenotypes were corrected by Unc-5 silencing (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: Elav>UBQLN24XALS/shUnc-5 flies showed a significant increase in lifespan relative to Elav>UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to shLuci, with the effect being most pronounced in female flies.
claims.source: Elav>UBQLN24XALS/shUnc-5 flies showed a significant increase in lifespan relative to Elav>UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to shLuci, with the effect being most pronounced in female flies (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Unc-5 knockdown modestly increased the lifespan of Elav-Gal4 male flies relative to Elav-Gal4/shLuci flies.
claims.source: Unc-5 knockdown also modestly increased the lifespan of Elav-Gal4 male flies relative to Elav-Gal4/shLuci flies while having no impact on lifespan of Elav-Gal4 female flies (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Unc-5 knockdown had no impact on lifespan of Elav-Gal4 female flies.
claims.source: Unc-5 knockdown also modestly increased the lifespan of Elav-Gal4 male flies relative to Elav-Gal4/shLuci flies while having no impact on lifespan of Elav-Gal4 female flies (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Aberrant Unc-5 signaling contributes to neuronal phenotypes in UBQLN24XALS flies.
claims.source: Altogether, these experiments suggest that aberrant Unc-5 signaling contributes to neuronal phenotypes in UBQLN24XALS flies.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined Unc-5 experiments.

claims.claim: The overlapping genetic interval spanned by the UBQLN24XALS suppressors Exel6038 and r10 contains beat-1b and beat-1c, two members of the beaten path (beat) family of axon guidance genes.
claims.source: Interestingly, the overlapping genetic interval spanned by the UBQLN24XALS suppressors Exel6038 and r10 contains beat-1b and beat-1c, two members of the beaten path (beat) family of axon guidance genes (Figure 5A–C; Vactor et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genetic mapping data shown in Figure 5A–C and a citation.

claims.claim: Neuronally expressed Beat proteins regulate motor axon guidance and defasciculation in response to Sidestep (Side) ligands expressed on target substrates.
claims.source: Neuronally expressed Beat proteins regulate motor axon guidance and defasciculation in response to Sidestep (Side) ligands expressed on target substrates (Fambrough and Goodman, 1996; Sink et al., 2001; Siebert et al., 2009; de Jong et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing Beat protein function.

claims.claim: UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to a Beat-1b shRNA line exhibited less severe eye degeneration than UBQLN24XALS flies expressing shRNAs targeting luciferase, mCherry, or beat-1c.
claims.source: UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to a Beat-1b shRNA line exhibited less severe eye degeneration than UBQLN24XALS flies expressing shRNAs targeting luciferase, mCherry, or beat-1c (Figure 5D, E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D, E and F.

claims.claim: GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies heterozygous for a p-element insertion in the beat-1b ORF exhibited improved eye phenotype relative to control GMR>UBQLN24XALS controls.
claims.source: GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies heterozygous for a p-element insertion in the beat-1b ORF also exhibited improved eye phenotype relative to control GMR>UBQLN24XALS controls (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Beat-1b signaling contributes to UBQLN2 toxicity.
claims.source: These findings support the idea that Beat-1b signaling contributes to UBQLN2 toxicity and further implicate axonal guidance defects as a contributing pathomechanism to UBQLN2-associated neurodegeneration.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the Beat-1b experiments.

claims.claim: Axonal guidance defects are a contributing pathomechanism to UBQLN2-associated neurodegeneration.
claims.source: These findings support the idea that Beat-1b signaling contributes to UBQLN2 toxicity and further implicate axonal guidance defects as a contributing pathomechanism to UBQLN2-associated neurodegeneration.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the identification of multiple axon guidance genes as modifiers.

claims.claim: CRISPR/CAS9 was employed to introduce ALS-associated mutations into the X-linked UBQLN2 gene in neonatal male induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).
claims.source: We employed CRISPR/CAS9 to introduce ALS-associated mutations into the X-linked UBQLN2 gene in neonatal male induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) (WC031i-5907-6, see Materials and methods, and Du et al., 2015).

results.result: UBQLN24XALS exhibits heat stress-dependent toxicity in Drosophila eyes. At 29°C, GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies show a rough eye phenotype with depigmentation and loss of ommatidial facets, while no overt phenotype is observed at 22°C. UBQLN24XALS is significantly less soluble than UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H at both temperatures, but the relative proportion of insoluble protein is comparable, suggesting aggregation alone does not fully explain enhanced toxicity. Protein expression levels are similar across genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C42-C50 provide converging evidence from eye morphology (Figure 1B), protein solubility assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), and mass spectrometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) demonstrating heat stress-dependent toxicity of UBQLN24XALS. The data show clear phenotypic differences at 29°C versus 22°C, with appropriate controls and quantification. The inference that aggregation alone cannot explain toxicity (C46) is supported by the observation that insoluble fractions are proportionally similar at both temperatures despite different phenotypic outcomes.

results.result: GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibit distinct transcriptomic changes compared to UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H flies. RNA-Seq analysis revealed 629 genes uniquely changed in UBQLN24XALS flies at 29°C (402 upregulated, 227 downregulated). Downregulated genes include those involved in eye development and phototransduction, while upregulated genes include innate immunity genes and heat shock proteins. This distinct gene expression signature correlates with the severe eye phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C63 are supported by RNA-Seq data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR <0.05) and biological replicates. The transcriptomic analysis provides molecular context for the observed phenotypes, with GO analysis supporting functional interpretations. The inference that UBQLN2 overexpression impacts cellular regulation (C52) is reasonable given the hundreds of gene expression changes observed.

results.result: A genetic deficiency screen in Drosophila identified 35 modifier loci for UBQLN2ALS toxicity. The UBQLN24XALS screen identified 7 suppressors and 23 enhancers (including 15 lethal enhancers), while the UBQLN2P497H screen identified 6 enhancers, two of which overlapped with the UBQLN24XALS screen. All enhancers of UBQLN2P497H also enhanced UBQLN2WT phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68, C148 describe the genetic screen methodology and results shown in Figure 2A-D. The screen design is appropriate with adequate coverage (194 lines spanning 85% of chromosome 2), and results are presented with clear phenotypic scoring. Secondary validation screens were performed to confirm modifiers. The observation that P497H enhancers also affect wild-type (C68) suggests these may represent general UBQLN2 modifiers rather than mutation-specific effects.

results.result: Rab5 is a mutation-independent modulator of UBQLN2 toxicity. Rab5 knockdown causes hyperpigmented eye phenotypes in flies expressing UBQLN2WT, UBQLN2P497H, and UBQLN24XALS at 29°C, with temperature-dependent effects. Rab5 overexpression partially rescues eye phenotypes without affecting UBQLN2 expression levels. These findings suggest UBQLN2 overexpression interferes with endolysosomal function.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C77, C151-C152 are supported by genetic interaction data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing consistent effects of Rab5 manipulation across multiple UBQLN2 alleles. The bidirectional effects (knockdown enhances, overexpression rescues) strengthen the conclusion. Controls showing no effect on UBQLN2 expression (C75) rule out indirect effects through protein levels. The inference about endolysosomal dysfunction (C77, C151) is reasonable and supported by citation to congruent work (C152).

results.result: The transcriptional elongation factor lilli suppresses UBQLN24XALS toxicity. A lilli LOF allele diminishes UBQLN24XALS eye toxicity to a similar extent as lilli-spanning deficiencies, without affecting UBQLN2 protein levels. lilli was previously shown to suppress TDP-43 and C9ORF72 DPR toxicity in Drosophila, suggesting it may be a general suppressor of neurodegeneration-associated protein toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81, C153-C156 are supported by genetic mapping data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and appropriate controls showing no effect on UBQLN2 expression (C155). The convergence with prior studies on TDP-43 and C9ORF72 (C79, C154) strengthens the conclusion about general suppressor function. However, the mechanism remains speculative (C156), as transcriptional suppression is ruled out but alternative mechanisms are not tested.

results.result: Unc-5 and its coreceptor frazzled/DCC modulate UBQLN24XALS toxicity in Drosophila eyes. Two Unc-5 LOF alleles and three RNAi lines diminish the rough eye phenotype without affecting UBQLN2 expression. Frazzled/DCC silencing similarly rescues the phenotype. The genetic interaction appears specific to UBQLN2, as Unc-5 knockdown does not affect FUS-associated eye phenotypes. These findings suggest signaling through Unc-5/Frazzled potentiates UBQLN24XALS toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C88, C157-C161 are supported by genetic interaction data (Figure 3) using multiple independent alleles and RNAi lines, strengthening confidence in the results. The specificity control with FUS (C84) is important for ruling out general effects on eye degeneration. The inference about Unc-5/Frazzled signaling (C88) is reasonable given the rescue by both components. However, the mechanism remains speculative (C159-C161), as the relative contributions of axon guidance versus apoptosis functions are not distinguished.

results.result: Unc-5 silencing rescues motor and lifespan phenotypes in UBQLN24XALS flies. Unc-5 knockdown partially reverses climbing defects in D42>UBQLN24XALS flies (with sex-specific effects for one RNAi line), corrects NMJ abnormalities including satellite bouton numbers, and significantly increases lifespan of Elav>UBQLN24XALS flies, particularly in females. These findings suggest aberrant Unc-5 signaling contributes to neuronal phenotypes beyond the eye.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96 are supported by multiple functional assays (Figure 4) including climbing behavior, NMJ morphology, and lifespan analysis. The use of multiple Unc-5 RNAi lines and appropriate controls strengthens the conclusions. Sex-specific effects (C90, C93-C95) are noted but not fully explained. The convergence of rescue effects across multiple phenotypic readouts (eye, motor, NMJ, lifespan) strongly supports the inference that Unc-5 signaling contributes to UBQLN2 toxicity (C96).

results.result: The axon guidance gene beat-1b suppresses UBQLN24XALS toxicity. Beat-1b knockdown and a p-element insertion in beat-1b reduce eye degeneration in UBQLN24XALS flies, while beat-1c knockdown has no effect. Beat proteins regulate motor axon guidance through interactions with Sidestep ligands. These findings further implicate axonal guidance defects as a pathomechanism in UBQLN2-associated neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102, C162-C164 are supported by genetic mapping and RNAi data (Figure 5) with appropriate specificity controls (beat-1c, luciferase, mCherry). The convergence with Unc-5/frazzled findings strengthens the conclusion about axon guidance defects (C102). However, the relevance to human disease is uncertain (C164) given weak homology to mammalian proteins (C163). The result would be strengthened by functional validation of axon guidance defects.

results.result: CRISPR-generated iPSC lines with endogenous UBQLN2 mutations show normal expression and localization under basal conditions. UBQLN2P497H, UBQLN22XALS, and UBQLN24XALS exhibit comparable expression and RIPA solubility to UBQLN2WT in undifferentiated iPSCs, with no detectable cytosolic aggregates. UBQLN2I498X is undetectable by Western blot, suggesting it is a null allele. These findings indicate endogenous ALS mutations are insufficient to promote UBQLN2 aggregation in undifferentiated iPSCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C110 are supported by Western blot and immunostaining data (Figure 6A-B) from CRISPR-edited iPSC lines. The methodology is appropriate and controls (UBQLN2I498X as null) are included. The inference that endogenous mutations are insufficient for aggregation in iPSCs (C109) is supported by the data, though this may reflect the undifferentiated state rather than a general property. The conclusion would be strengthened by validation in multiple clones for each genotype.

results.result: Endogenous UBQLN24XALS exhibits altered protein folding in iPSCs. Limited proteolysis with chymotrypsin reveals a unique fragmentation pattern for UBQLN24XALS compared to UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H, suggesting the endogenous 4XALS mutant protein is misfolded, consistent with prior findings using purified protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are supported by limited proteolysis data (Figure 6C) and citation to prior work. The assay is appropriate for detecting conformational differences. However, the interpretation that the unique fragmentation pattern indicates misfolding (C112) is an inference that could be strengthened by additional biophysical characterization. The result is consistent with the aggregation propensity of UBQLN24XALS.

results.result: UBQLN2ALS iPSCs exhibit lysosomal defects that are unmasked by autophagy inhibition. BafA1 treatment decreases solubility of all UBQLN2 proteins, with the strongest effect on UBQLN24XALS, which remains insoluble after washout. UBQLN2 partially colocalizes with LAMP1 but not Rab5. UBQLN2P497H and UBQLN24XALS iPSCs show significantly elevated lysosome abundance and size compared to wild-type, with UBQLN24XALS exhibiting the most severe enlargement. LC3 lipidation is comparable across genotypes, suggesting similar autophagic flux.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C121, C165-C166 are supported by biochemical fractionation (Figure 6D-E), colocalization studies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B), and LysoTracker analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D). The use of BafA1 to unmask aggregation propensity is appropriate. The lysosomal enlargement phenotype is quantified with statistical analysis. However, the interpretation of LC3 levels as indicating similar autophagic flux (C116) is indirect and could be confounded by other factors affecting LC3 lipidation. The convergence of multiple assays supports endolysosomal dysfunction (C121).

results.result: UBQLN24XALS forms discrete aggregates in differentiated motor neurons. In iMNs, UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H show diffuse localization, while UBQLN24XALS forms discrete aggregates distributed throughout cell bodies, axons, and growth cones. Aggregation is observed in two independent UBQLN24XALS clones. UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H are evenly distributed in growth cone lamellipodia and filopodia, while UBQLN24XALS shows weaker lamellipodial staining with occasional bright aggregates in ~50% of growth cones. DCC localization to filopodial spikes is not affected by the UBQLN24XALS mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C127 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 7A-B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, Figure 7—figure supplement 2) from differentiated iMNs. The observation of aggregates in two independent clones (C124) strengthens confidence that this is not a clonal artifact. The quantification of aggregate frequency in growth cones (C126) provides rigor. The finding that DCC localization is unaffected (C127) is an important control suggesting the mutation does not globally disrupt growth cone structure.

results.result: UBQLN24XALS iMNs exhibit reduced neurite complexity. Sholl analysis reveals UBQLN24XALS iMNs have significantly reduced total neurite length, primary neurite length, and branch length compared to UBQLN2WT, manifesting as increased Sholl decay. In contrast, UBQLN2P497H iMNs show neurite length and complexity comparable to wild-type, indicating the clinical P497H mutation alone is insufficient to disrupt neurite growth dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C131 are supported by quantitative Sholl analysis (Figure 7D) with large sample sizes (>100 neurons) and appropriate statistical testing. The methodology is well-described and appropriate for assessing neurite complexity. The finding that P497H does not affect neurite growth (C130-C131) is important for distinguishing mutation-specific effects and suggests the 4XALS mutation has more severe consequences than single clinical mutations.

results.result: Autophagy inhibition increases UBQLN24XALS aggregation in iMNs. BafA1 treatment strongly increases the size and number of UBQLN24XALS aggregates in two independent clones, with minimal effects on UBQLN2WT or UBQLN2P497H. BafA1-induced aggregates strongly colocalize with p62 and often colocalize with or are adjacent to LAMP1-positive lysosomes, but show weak colocalization with Rab5 or LC3. These findings suggest the autophagy pathway suppresses endogenous UBQLN24XALS aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C136 are supported by immunostaining and colocalization analysis (Figure 8) with quantification and statistical testing. The use of two independent clones strengthens confidence. The colocalization analysis with multiple markers (p62, LAMP1, Rab5, LC3) provides mechanistic insight. However, the inference that autophagy suppresses aggregation (C136) is based on pharmacological inhibition and could be strengthened by genetic manipulation of autophagy components.

results.result: UNC5B and DCC knockdown rescues neurite defects in UBQLN24XALS iMNs without affecting aggregation. shRNA-mediated knockdown of UNC5B or DCC (40-60% reduction confirmed by qPCR) significantly increases total neurite length, primary neurite length, and branch length in UBQLN24XALS iMNs compared to non-targeting control. Neither knockdown affects the size or number of UBQLN24XALS aggregates, suggesting they influence toxicity pathways downstream of aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C141 are supported by qPCR validation of knockdown (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-B), neurite analysis (Figure 9A), and aggregate quantification (Figure 9—figure supplement 2). The finding that rescue occurs without affecting aggregates (C140-C141) is important for distinguishing aggregation-dependent and aggregation-independent toxicity mechanisms. The convergence with Drosophila findings strengthens the conclusion about conserved mechanisms.

results.result: UBQLN24XALS iMNs exhibit growth cone defects that are rescued by UNC5B/DCC knockdown. UBQLN24XALS iMNs show a high proportion of blunt-end termini versus growth cones, observed in two independent clones, suggesting defective growth cone elaboration. UNC5B or DCC knockdown in UBQLN24XALS iMNs results in supernumerary growth cones along neurites and increased growth cone size and abundance. These findings suggest aberrant DCC-UNC5 signaling suppresses growth cone elaboration and that axon guidance defects contribute to toxicity in both fly and iMN models.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 are supported by growth cone morphology analysis (Figure 9B-D) with quantification and statistical testing. The observation in two independent clones (C143) strengthens confidence. The rescue of growth cone defects by UNC5B/DCC knockdown (C144) provides strong evidence for the proposed mechanism. The inference about conserved mechanisms across flies and human cells (C146) is well-supported by the convergence of results across model systems.

results.result: Altered growth cone dynamics and endolysosomal dysfunction are conserved pathomechanisms in UBQLN2-associated ALS/FTD. The combined findings from Drosophila genetic screens and human iPSC/iMN studies support roles for endolysosomal dysfunction (via Rab5) and axon guidance defects (via Unc-5/DCC) as disease drivers. The UBQLN24XALS toxicity mechanism is at least partially conserved between flies and humans, as demonstrated by rescue of phenotypes in both systems through manipulation of orthologous genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C39, C147, C171, C186 represent the main conclusions synthesizing results across model systems. The conclusions are well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches: genetic screens in flies identifying Rab5 and Unc-5 as modifiers, functional validation in fly motor neurons and lifespan assays, and rescue of neurite and growth cone defects in human iMNs by UNC5B/DCC knockdown. The conservation across species strengthens confidence in the relevance to human disease. However, the mechanisms linking UBQLN2 aggregation to aberrant UNC5/DCC signaling remain incompletely defined.

results.result: Study limitations and alternative interpretations. The authors acknowledge several limitations: (1) UBQLN24XALS is not a bona fide disease allele and may elicit toxicities unrelated to clinical mutations; (2) overexpression may cause disease-nonspecific toxicities affecting genetic screens; (3) axon guidance genes may be most relevant during development; (4) iPSC/iMN models may not capture age-dependent abnormalities. The enhanced toxicity of UBQLN24XALS may be due to overwhelming proteostasis machinery, and soluble forms of mutant UBQLN2 may also contribute to toxicity, particularly through endolysosomal dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C150, C168-C170, C187-C190 represent appropriate acknowledgment of study limitations and alternative interpretations. The authors correctly note that UBQLN24XALS is an artificial construct (C188) and that overexpression models have inherent limitations (C187). The speculation about mechanisms (C149, C168-C170) is reasonable given the data. These limitations do not invalidate the main findings but appropriately contextualize the conclusions and suggest directions for future work.
